Exceptionally well reported, and useful to the survey as a counter-example: it states everything the schema asks for, including the coupling refractive index, which almost nothing else does. Two of its own observations support the premise of this study directly. First, the authors report a 'geometry effect': for most ingots the plate-shaped samples give the highest light collection, so the same material yields different numbers depending on the shape cut from it. Second, light yield varies along a single crystal fibre (9,978 to 9,191 ph/MeV, and elsewhere a 4.3 %/cm gradient), so the number depends on where in the crystal the interaction happened. column18: absolute: single-photoelectron calibration, divided by QE and by a Geant4-simulated light collection efficiency
column25: Cryostat geometry, LCE 24 percent. PRIOR ART FOR PAPER 0'S METHOD. This paper already does what we proposed: it divides the measured photoelectron count by the PMT quantum efficiency AND by a light-collection efficiency obtained from a Geant4 optical simulation (version 10.6.p01, G4OpticalPhysics, UNIFIED surface model), to recover an intrinsic photon yield. LCE was 81 percent with the crystal coupled directly to the PMT window and 24 percent inside the optical cryostat. They quote a 5 percent relative uncertainty on the simulated LCE. That figure is the point of contact with this study: our own one-at-a-time scan of the optical inputs for NaI(Tl) -- refractive index, bulk absorption, emission band shape -- moves the light-collection efficiency by 42 percent across models consistent with the available measurements and 76 percent across what the literature actually uses. A 5 percent uncertainty on a simulated LCE is therefore hard to sustain unless the optical inputs are pinned down far better than they are for NaI, which is among the best-characterised scintillators there is. The same paper reports 50,300 +- 4,800 ph/MeV for the same crystal coupled directly to the PMT window (LCE 81 percent) -- two configurations, two numbers, 6 percent apart. An earlier independent study is cited at 33,900 ph/MeV at room temperature for this material, 57 percent below this work.

column18: absolute: measured photoelectrons divided by QE and by a Monte-Carlo light collection efficiency (MCRIM); cross-checked against a CaWO4 reference
column25: The cleanest quantitative demonstration of this project's premise that the survey has turned up. The SAME crystal, in the SAME setup, with a 0.05 mm gap held by wires, gives 14.3 +- 0.2 detected photons with the gap empty and 24.5 +- 0.4 with the gap filled with Cargille optical gel (n = 1.46) -- a 71 percent change from the optical coupling alone. The authors compute light collection efficiencies of 0.25 and 0.43 for the two cases and divide them out to recover one intrinsic yield. Unusually complete reporting: surfaces polished to a stated 50 nm roughness, measured transmittance 76 percent at the 540 nm emission peak (96 percent after correcting for multiple reflection, giving an absorption coefficient of 0.039 /cm), refractive index 2.01 cited, no reflector used, PMT quantum efficiency from the manufacturer. This is prior art for the correction protocol and a model of how to report it; note that the quoted total uncertainty is 16 percent, several times the 5 percent claimed for a simulated LCE in arXiv:2509.26416.

The paper also compares optical grease against an air gap and finds an improvement of about 80 percent (a factor ~1.7 in the conclusions) -- independently consistent with arXiv:1303.5952, which finds 71 percent from the same change on a completely different crystal. Charge integrated over 50-300 ns; yield computed from the fitted peak charge, the stated PMT gain of 3.8e6 and the 511 keV annihilation photon energy. Note the unit: photoelectrons per MeV, which carries the PMT quantum efficiency and this setup's light collection. This row: Teflon wrapping, the best of the three.

column18: absolute, reconstructed from detected photons by hand-applied geometric factors
column25: A textbook case of why this project exists, and the authors are commendably open about it. They detect ~6,700 photons/MeV on the SiPM ACTIVE AREA, scale to ~18,600 for the whole crystal face the sensor covers, then 'since the crystal face opposite to the SiPM was bare, we can conservatively add another factor 2', arriving at ~37,200 photons/MeV -- which they note is 'fairly compatible with the nominal value of ~40000 indicated by the crystal producer'. That is a total correction factor of about 5.6, one element of which is a round factor of 2 applied by judgement, landing on the vendor's figure. The correction is exactly the right thing to attempt; doing it with a simulated light-collection efficiency instead of round numbers is the difference this study is about. They also note they neglected light dispersion on the coated side faces.

column25: Maximum over a 94-293 K scan, reached at 238 K and 34.5 percent above the room-temperature value -- so even for one crystal in one setup, 'the light yield' is a curve, not a number. Cut from ingot NaI-036 of the COSINE-200 low-background programme, several layers of soft PTFE around the exposed faces, two SiPMs directly on the end faces with no coupling compound mentioned. Compare with ANAIS (arXiv:1703.01262), which reports about 15,000 photoelectrons/MeV for 12.5 kg crystals read by PMTs: similar number, utterly different detector, and the units hide both the photodetector response and the light collection.

column25: A useful counter-example to the disagreements this survey has been documenting. Cryogenic undoped CsI has been measured by several groups at 26.0 PE/keVee (1.0 kg, PMT readout, Jin Liu et al.), 28.7 and 29.3 PE/keVee (3.3 kg, dual-ended PMT, this work) and 30.1 PE/keVee (0.5 kg, SiPM arrays, arXiv:2212.11515) -- a 16 percent spread across different masses and different photodetectors. When a community states its conditions and measures the same quantity, it agrees. The factor-of-two and factor-of-four disagreements found elsewhere in this corpus are not inevitable. Wrapped in Teflon and black paper, with the coupling areas also wrapped in Teflon. A second crystal in the same work gave 28.7 +- 0.9 PE/keVee.
